L0@P0: REDUCTIVE GROUP SCHEMES
L1@P0: Brian Conrad
L2@P0: Abstract. — We develop the relative theory of reductive group schemes,
L3@P0: using dynamic techniques and algebraic spaces to streamline the original development in SGA3.
L4@P0: R´esum´e. — Nous d´eveloppons la th´eorie relative des sch´emas en groupes
L5@P0: r´eductifs, `a l’aide da techniques dynamiques et des espaces alg´ebriques afin de
L6@P0: simplifier le d´eveloppement original dans SGA3.
L7@P0: To the memory of Robert Steinberg
L8@P0: Introduction
L9@P0: These notes present the theory of reductive group schemes, simplifying the
L10@P0: original proofs via tools developed after 1963 (see “What’s new?” at the end
L11@P0: of this Introduction). We assume familiarity with the structure theory over
L12@P0: an algebraically closed field k (as developed in [Bo91], [Hum87], [Spr]), but
L13@P0: a review is given in § 1 to fix terminology, set everything in the framework of
L14@P0: k-schemes (rather than classical varieties), and provide a convenient reference
L15@P0: for the scheme-theoretic developments.
L16@P0: We give complete proofs of the main results in the theory (conjugacy theorems, scheme of maximal tori, construction of root groups and root datum,
L17@P0: structure of open cell, parameterization of parabolics, schemes of Borel and
L18@P0: parabolic subgroups, Existence and Isomorphism theorems, existence of automorphism scheme), apart from some calculations with low-rank root systems.
L19@P0: We do not assume the Existence and Isomorphism Theorems over a general
L20@P0: algebraically closed field k because the scheme-theoretic approach proves these
L21@P0: over any non-empty base scheme granting only the Existence Theorem over
L22@P0: k = C (which we prove in Appendix D).
L23@P0: 
L24@P0-1: c 2014, Soci´et´e math´ematique de France2 BRIAN CONRAD
L25@P1: Although the structure theory of connected reductive groups is developed
L26@P1: over a general field in [Bo91] and [Spr], we take on faith only the case of an
L27@P1: algebraically closed ground field (as in [SGA3] via its reliance on [BIBLE]).
L28@P1: Some results are proved here in less generality than in [SGA3], since our
L29@P1: aim is to reach the structure theory of reductive group schemes as quickly as
L30@P1: possible. In a small number of places we refer to [SGA3] for omitted proofs,
L31@P1: and the interested reader can readily check that this does not create circular
L32@P1: arguments in our development of the general theory.
L33@P1: Background. — We assume familiarity with smooth and ´etale morphisms
L34@P1: (e.g., functorial criteria for each; cf. [BLR, 2.1–2.2]), faithfully flat descent
L35@P1: (see [BLR, 6.1–6.2]), and the functorial approach to group schemes (e.g.,
L36@P1: scheme-theoretic kernels, intersections of closed subgroup schemes, and quotient morphisms via sheaves for a Grothendieck topology). We also use Cartier
L37@P1: duality for finite flat commutative group schemes (of finite presentation).
L38@P1: In the arguments after § 1 we use multiplicative type group schemes [SGA3,
L39@P1: IX, X]. This material is covered in Appendix B, building on Oesterl´e’s lectures
L40@P1: [Oes]. We use a more restricted notion of “multiplicative type” than in [SGA3]
L41@P1: and [Oes]. In these notes, by definition multiplicative type groups are required
L42@P1: to be of finite type over the base, and are required to split fppf-locally on the
L43@P1: base: they are fppf-local forms of diagonalizable groups of finite type. The
L44@P1: fpqc topology is used instead of the fppf topology in the definition in [SGA3,
L45@P1: IX, 1.1] and [Oes] (allowing fpqc groups that are not of finite type). Our
L46@P1: restriction to the fppf topology is harmless, as we explain in Appendix B
L47@P1: (due to the “finite type” requirement that we impose). We often use that
L48@P1: multiplicative type groups are necessarily split ´etale-locally on the base. It
L49@P1: is inconvenient to include this in the definition of “multiplicative type”, so a
L50@P1: proof of ´etale-local splitting is given in Proposition B.3.4 (as a mild variant of
L51@P1: the proof of an analogous result in [SGA3, IX, 4.5]). The equivalence with
L52@P1: fpqc-local triviality (under a finite-type hypothesis on the group) is proved in
L53@P1: Corollary B.4.2(1) but is never used.
L54@P1: We require the notion of Lie algebra for a group scheme (not necessarily
L55@P1: smooth). A reference that covers what we need (and beyond) is [CGP, A.7].
L56@P1: One of the properties we use for the Lie functor is that it commutes with fiber
L57@P1: products of groups (and so is left exact), as is verified by considering points
L58@P1: valued in the dual numbers over the base.
L59@P1: For a reader unfamiliar with algebraic spaces, in a few places it will be
L60@P1: necessary to accept that algebraic spaces are a useful mechanism to equip
L61@P1: certain set-valued functors with enough “geometric structure” that it makes
L62@P1: sense to carry over concepts for schemes (e.g., properness, flatness, quasifiniteness, etc.) to such functors; an excellent reference for this is [Knut]. All
L63@P1-2: algebraic spaces we use will almost immediately be proved to be schemes, soREDUCTIVE GROUP SCHEMES 3
L64@P2: our use of algebraic spaces will be similar to the use of distributions to provide
L65@P2: function solutions to elliptic partial differential equations (i.e., they appear in
L66@P2: the middle of a construction, the end result of which is an object of a more
L67@P2: familiar type that we prefer to use).
L68@P2: Theory over a field. — In Example 5.3.9 we relate the approach in [SGA3]
L69@P2: to other constructions in the literature (e.g., [St67]) for the group of fieldvalued points of a split semisimple group. Many arithmetic applications (as
L70@P2: well as applications over R) require a structure theory for connected reductive
L71@P2: groups over general fields k without assuming the existence of a split (geometrically) maximal k-torus. Such a structure theory is due to Borel and Tits (see
L72@P2: [BoTi] and [Bo91, § 20–24]), and is not discussed here. In [SGA3, XXVI,
L73@P2: 6.16–6.18, § 7] and [G, § 4–§ 5] the Borel–Tits theory is partially generalized to
L74@P2: reductive groups over connected semi-local non-empty schemes; see [PS] for
L75@P2: recent work in this direction.
L76@P2: There is a result at the foundation of the Borel–Tits structure theory for
L77@P2: which we do provide a proof: Grothendieck’s theorem [SGA3, XIV, 1.1] (later
L78@P2: proved in more elementary terms by Borel and Springer) that any smooth affine
L79@P2: group G over a field k admits a k-torus T ⊂ G such that Tk
L80@P2: is maximal in Gk.
L81@P2: This existence result implies that for every k-torus T0in G not contained in a
L82@P2: strictly larger k-torus and for every extension field K/k, T0
L83@P2: K is not contained in
L84@P2: a strictly larger K-torus of GK (see Remark A.1.2 for a proof). In particular,
L85@P2: the concept of “maximal k-torus” in a smooth affine group over k is insensitive
L86@P2: to ground field extension. (We only use this in the trivial case k = k.)
L87@P2: Since Grothendieck’s existence theorem for maximal tori over arbitrary
L88@P2: fields is not needed in the development of the theory of reductive groups over
L89@P2: general schemes, we have relegated our discussion of his theorem to Appendix
L90@P2: A (which provides a scheme-theoretic version of the Borel–Springer proof of
L91@P2: Grothendieck’s theorem). What matters for our purposes is the existence of a
L92@P2: “geometrically maximal” torus defined over a finite separable extension of the
L93@P2: ground field. We present Grothendieck’s construction of such a torus, using

L7@P0: 0. Introduction
L8@P0: Let k be a field with separable closure ks and Galois group Γk = Gal(ks/k).
L9@P0: We assume that k is perfect throughout this introduction; then ks is an algebraic
L10@P0: closure of k. Let G be an algebraic group over k. (By this we always mean a
L11@P0: smooth group scheme of finite type over Spec k.) Recall that a homogeneous Gspace is a non-empty smooth algebraic scheme X together with a (right) action
L12@P0: by G on X, both X and the action being defined over k, such that the action of
L13@P0: G(ks) on X(ks) is transitive. The G-space X is called a principal homogeneous Gspace (or a G-torsor) if in addition this last action is free, i.e. has trivial stabilizer
L14@P0: subgroups. The non-abelian Galois cohomology set H1(k, G)= H1(Γk,G(ks)) is
L15@P0: the set of isomorphism classes of principal homogeneous G-spaces over k. A wellknown theorem of Steinberg (“Conjecture I” of Serre; see [S2], III, §2.3, Thm. 10
L16@P0: )
L17@P0: asserts that when k has cohomological dimension at most one (cd(k) ≤ 1) and G is
L18@P0: connected and linear, the cohomology set H1(k, G) is trivial. In other words, each
L19@P0: principal homogeneous G-space is trivial, which means, has a k-point.
L20@P0: There is a general definition of the second non-abelian cohomology set in terms of
L21@P0: gerbes (by Grothendieck, Dedecker, Giraud [G]; see also Deligne-Milne [DM], Breen
L22@P0: [Br]). Springer [Sp] constructed a non-abelian H2-set in terms of group extensions;
L23@P0: this set has an equivalent description in terms of 2-cocycles. His approach was
L24@P0: recently taken up again by Borovoi [B1]. Here is a brief review of this setup: Given
L25@P0: an algebraic group G over ks, let SOut(G/k) be the quotient of the group SAut(G/k)
L26@P0: of k-semilinear automorphisms of G by the subgroup Int(G) of inner automorphisms
L27@P0: of G.A k-kernel in G is a homomorphic section κ of the natural homomorphism
L28@P0: SOut(G/k) → Γk which satisfies a certain continuity condition. (The notion of
L29@P0: continuity is delicate.) The set H2(k, G, κ) classifies group extensions of G(ks) by
L30@P0: Γk compatible with the kernel κ. It may be empty. If it is not, it is a principal
L31@P0: homogeneous set under the abelian group H2(k,Z), where Z is the center of G,
L32@P0: considered as an algebraic group over k by means of κ. The elements of H2(k, G, κ)
L33@P0: which correspond to split extensions are called neutral. The set of neutral elements
L34@P0: is denoted by N2(k, G, κ), and the kernel κ is said to be trivial if there exists a
L35@P0: neutral element. Theorem 3.5 of [Sp] — attributed to Grothendieck — asserts that
L36@P0: if k is perfect with cd(k) ≤ 1 and G is any algebraic group over ks, then any k-kernel
L37@P0: κ in G is trivial, and H2(k, G, κ) consists of a single element which is (therefore)
L38@P0: neutral.

L53@P1: (perfect) field k with cd(k) = 1, each homogeneous space under an algebraic group

L5@P0: Abstract. Let p be a prime. Let (R, m) be a regular local ring of mixed
L6@P0: characteristic (0, p) and absolute index of ramification e. We provide general
L7@P0: criteria of when each abelian scheme over Spec R \ {m} extends to an abelian
L8@P0: scheme over Spec R. We show that such extensions always exist if e ≤ p−1, exist
L9@P0: in most cases if p ≤ e ≤ 2p − 3, and do not exist in general if e ≥ 2p − 2. The
L10@P0: case e ≤ p − 1 implies the uniqueness of integral canonical models of Shimura
L11@P0: varieties over a discrete valuation ring O of mixed characteristic (0, p) and index

L13@P0: over O. If p > 2 and e = p − 1, the examples are new.
